fields.foundation: The Fatimid Caliphate grew not out of dynastic inheritance but out of a clandestine Ismaili missionary organisation, the da'wa, which spent decades preparing a revolution against the Sunni Abbasid order. The da'i Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i won the Kutama Berbers of Ifriqiya to the cause of a hidden imam whose identity was kept secret for security. In 909 his Kutama army overthrew the Aghlabid emirate, and the imam was retrieved from Sijilmasa and proclaimed caliph at Raqqada in January 910 as Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah, establishing a rival caliphate to Baghdad. Three conditions made the founding possible: a highly organised subversive network, a militarily capable Berber host people, and a theological claim tracing the imamate directly to the Prophet through his daughter Fatima. The empire was built on that claim. Every institution existed to defend it or to propagate it, and in the end failed to sustain it.
fields.socioeconomy: Egypt, conquered in 969 by the general Jawhar al-Siqilli, changed the caliphate's economy entirely. The Nile valley's agricultural surplus provided a stable revenue base that the arid Ifriqiyan heartland had never offered. Cairo was founded north of Fustat as a palatine capital, and the al-Azhar mosque was begun in 970. At the empire's peak around 1047, the Persian traveller Nasir-i Khusraw described great wealth: the caliph reportedly owned some 20,000 shops in Cairo from which he collected rent, along with numerous caravanserais and bathhouses that brought in continuous revenue. Egypt's geography made it the pivot of Red Sea to Mediterranean transit trade, connecting Indian Ocean spice networks to European markets, and taxation on this commerce was a principal source of income. The caliphate governed a majority Sunni Egyptian population while employing a cosmopolitan bureaucracy that included Christians and Jews in senior positions. This pragmatic tolerance sat uneasily with the dynasty's sectarian claims and was sharply interrupted by al-Hakim's persecutions.
fields.military: The Fatimid army was deliberately multinational, which was its strength in the field and in time its weakness. Kutama Berbers formed the original revolutionary core; Turkish slave soldiers, the ghilman, were recruited for their skill as mounted archers; Black African infantry from the Sudan formed a large and politically assertive contingent. Jawhar led the largely unopposed conquest of Egypt with a reported force exceeding 100,000, then repelled the Qarmatian counter-attack that threatened Cairo in its earliest years. Under al-Aziz, the caliphate defeated the Turkish commander Alptakin near Ramla in the late 970s and pressed its claims in Syria against local and Byzantine-backed rivals. The army's ethnic factionalism was never resolved. In the 1060s and early 1070s, rivalries among Berber, Turkish, and Sudanese units broke into open street warfare in Cairo, the vizierate changed hands dozens of times, and the institutions of government ceased to work together. Badr al-Jamali afterwards rebuilt the state, and the gates of Bab Zuwayla, Bab al-Futuh, and Bab al-Nasr that he built still stand. He restored order, but it was an order that depended on his own Armenian troops rather than the caliphate's composite army.
fields.governance: The Fatimid caliphate worked through two sets of institutions, an arrangement without parallel in the medieval Islamic world. The overt apparatus consisted of the caliph, the vizierate, and conventional provincial administration. The covert apparatus was the da'wa, the missionary network propagating Ismaili doctrine across Persia, Sind, Yemen, and Arabia under a chief missionary in Cairo. The office of vizier was formalised under Ya'qub ibn Killis, the first holder appointed by al-Aziz, and grew from that of an administrative coordinator into the seat of real executive power. By the late eleventh century, caliphs had become largely ceremonial figures. Badr al-Jamali, arriving in 1073, combined the posts of army commander, head of the missionary organisation, chief judge, and vizier. Real government was now concentrated in a military strongman, while the caliph retained only a theological function. The dual structure around which the empire had been designed had collapsed completely.
fields.impact: Al-Azhar, developed as a teaching institution from 988 onwards, became the most important centre of Islamic learning in the Arab world, a status it retains today although Saladin reversed its Ismaili orientation after 1171. The caliphate's control of the Red Sea trade corridor made Cairo the premier commercial metropolis of the Islamic world. It directed Indian Ocean commerce towards North African and European markets, and Mediterranean trade followed that pattern for generations. The da'wa's missionaries founded Ismaili communities in Yemen, Persia, and the Indian subcontinent that have lasted. The Nizari branch that split away following the 1094 succession crisis was led in Iran by Hasan-i Sabbah from the fortress of Alamut in the Alborz mountains. It gave rise to the Assassin tradition and to an Ismaili lineage whose imams, the Aga Khans, trace their institution in unbroken line directly to the Fatimid missionary apparatus.
fields.decline: The Fatimid collapse took a century and had no single breaking point. The Zirid defection of around 1048, when the Ifriqiyan governor al-Mu'izz ibn Badis abandoned Ismaili allegiance for Sunni orthodoxy, permanently cut off the caliphate's North African hinterland. The Mustansirite Hardship of the 1060s, seven years of catastrophically low Nile floods, brought famine and plague, depopulated Cairo, and broke the army into murderous factions. In the succession crisis of 1094, Vizier al-Afdal bypassed the designated heir Nizar in favour of al-Musta'li, which permanently split the Ismaili community and destroyed the da'wa's universal authority. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, and the last Levantine stronghold, Ascalon, fell in 1153. Saladin entered Egypt with the Zengid army in 1169, became vizier, replaced Ismaili judges with Sunni ones, and in September 1171 ordered the Friday prayer read in the name of the Abbasid caliph. The last caliph, al-Adid, died on 13 September 1171, reportedly unaware that his caliphate had already ceased to exist.
fields.summary: The Fatimid Caliphate was an empire whose political existence rested on a theological claim. Its end came not through military conquest but through the quiet exhaustion of that claim, which had made it possible in the first place.
fields.teaser: The Fatimid Caliphate was an Ismaili Shia dynasty that ruled much of North Africa and founded Cairo as its capital. Its al-Azhar mosque, begun in 970, remains a leading centre of Islamic learning today.
fields.t0: An Ismaili Shia caliphate born of a secret missionary network in North Africa, set up in 910 as a rival to Abbasid Baghdad.
fields.t1: From Cairo, which it founded, it controlled Red Sea to Mediterranean trade and built al-Azhar, still a leading centre of Islamic learning.
fields.t2: Famine, army factions and a schism in 1094 eroded it until Saladin quietly restored Abbasid prayers in 1171.
fields.dyk: The Nizari Ismailis who broke away after the 1094 succession crisis gave rise to the imams known today as the Aga Khans, a lineage tracing back to the Fatimid missionary network.
